newsitem.title: UK: Mark seen tarnished by stability pact in Dublin.
newsitem.headline: Mark seen tarnished by stability pact in Dublin.

text.p: A comprehensive European Union agreement this weekend on how to rein in annual budget deficits after monetary union will more than likely be negative for the German mark, currency analysts said.
There has been talk that an agreement on the so-called "stability pact" will bolster the mark by making the future single currency a more stable, credible unit.
But, the rules of thumb that currency investors have now arrived at mean that the nature of pact, not the pact itself, will be most important to the market reaction.

Current thinking reasons that a concrete agreement this week will almost certainly require German flexibility and undermine the mark as a result, analysts said. A pact completely on German lines would potentially be mark bullish but is less likely.

No final agreement in Dublin, on th other hand, and merely a committment to keep looking for a solution into the Dutch European presidency early next year will more than likely be an anti climax for the markets, they argue.

"If there is a stability pact that is perceived to be watered down, then all European currencies as a bloc will suffer against the dollar and outside currencies," said Lee Ferridge, treasury economist at NatWest Markets.

Ferridge said that if the strict German position wins out then peripheral European currencies, like the Italian lira and Spanish peseta, could lose out because they would then be less likely to go ahead with EMU as early as 1999.
Tnis could buoy the mark indirectly, he said, although the most likely outcome was that agreement is postponed.

"A non-hardline stability pact would re-accelerate the trend of mark weakness and return the bias toward the high-yielders (like the lira, peseta and Swedish crown)," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro.
The key is the likelihood of Germany easing its stance.

Germany's insistance on both steep and automatic post-EMU fines on member EMU member states who breach 3.0 percent annual deficit ceilings has not met with wide support, analysts said. The only country to fully support Germany is the Netherlands.

As a result, the only way there is going to be an EU-wide agreement this weekend is if there is more flexibility from Germany and an effective watering down of their extreme demands. This is not as unliklley as many in market have assumed, however, with EU diplomats indicating after last week's EU finance ministers meeting in Brussels that Germany had already softened its initial hardline bargaining position.

The sticking point has been Germany's insistance that exceptional economic circumstances allowing statess to avoid fines for excessive deficits be as extreme as four consecutive quarters of falling growth, or a drop of 2 percent in a year.

Yet, diplomats said this demand had already been cut back to 1.5 percent last week. They said Germany had also dropped its hardline demand for fines to kick in at 0.25 percent of gross domestic product and accepted 0.2 percent instead.
The French, on the other hand, are still opposed to the automatic nature of the fining and are arguing for the issue to be treated on a case-by-case basis.

"I think the Germans have given up the ghost on this one. The French and the rest of Europe are insisting on a softer Euro against the dollar and there has been no obvious or vocal objection from Germany," said Norfield at ABN Amro.
What is a possibiliy, analysts argue, is that compromise is reached by giving Germany close to what it wants on the numbers while assuaging France by not insisting the fines are automatic.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, currently president of the European Council, said in Paris today that states other than Germany agree there should be figures defining exceptional circumstances "don't want it to be absolutely automatic."
"It all hinges on assurances that the exceptional circumstances exception will not be used in a politically easy way."
Some currency analysts argue that barring a major breakdown of EU relations at the summit, the powerful EMU process leaves little of solace for the German currency.

"All in all, I really can't envisage any situation coming out of this weekend's summit that will prove either significantly or sustainably positive for the mark," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
